title: Composing: Central State, the Centrillions, Song of Her and Mutima
summary: McBee discusses learning piano in college, resurrecting Frank Foster's Centrillions, his first composition on Forest Flower, and Mutima as a composer's statement.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Yeah. On a personal note I was happy to see that a musician that was a housemate of mine at SUNY Fredonia played on your record, Onaje Allan Gumbs.

That was a rather exciting moment because actually I failed to mention to you that upon arrival in New York City I felt that I was more a composer than a performer. Because in college I mean upon arriving at school I had never played the piano before. I didn’t even know what that was as far as putting my fingers on the keyboard and making something happen. But as a potential music instructor the piano was the first assignment of study. So I fell in love with that and began, you know, exploring, and especially with the understanding that the great Frank Foster who was a previous graduate of my school which is Central State University in Southwest Ohio. He had — his big band had won the national big band contest for quality performance, which brought a bit of acclaim to that little school in Southwest Ohio.

So upon hearing some of my little tunes that I had begun to create, the students chose me as, you know, one that might want to resurrect the Centrillions, the band that Frank Foster left, and so we brought out, we were give his compositions and we played a few concerts around, and my conducting. So I found a thrill to discover things on the piano that might give me reason to express myself in that medium. So I spent a lot of time on the piano getting my chord changes and I began to write tunes. So when I first arrived in New York City quite frankly I was a pretty decent composer. Speaking of Charles Lloyd, my very
first composition that I wrote upon arriving in New York City that first year was a tune called “Song of Her.”
Which was on the Forest Flower record is that correct?

Right? And so I was more excited about having my tune on the recording rather than what it really meant. You know I called my mother and said, “Mom, you know, they recorded my music.” And to this day it’s supposed to be one of my most appreciated tunes. But so throughout, until now, have always sat at the piano and I’ve collected a lot of music. So when “Mutima” came about this was the opportunity for me to demonstrate to the world at large that I was a composer not just a bass player. I had a chance to realize on the recording to the public that there were other levels of thought compositionally that I felt pretty good about.

I watched that lovely video of you for your 84th birthday and there were some great quotes in there, one of which was when I feel something I run to the piano, something like that. Yeah. I also loved that moment, I had to laugh because there was a moment where you were rehearsing a group with those three wonderful saxophone players and one of them was working on his part and he kept playing this interval and apparently it was wrong. And you said something like, “Now I know why I shouldn’t have jumped out of bed and wrote this” or something.
